thread.title: Will IPO hopes for Uber, Lyft and Airbnb be dashed by today’s stock market plunge?

author: Mark Calvey
title: Will IPO hopes for Uber, Lyft and Airbnb be dashed by today’s stock market plunge?
text: – Senior Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Dec 4, 2018, 2:57pm PST Updated Dec 4, 2018, 6:26pm PST Stocks plunged on Wall Street Tuesday, casting a huge shadow over next year’s IPO ambitions for some of the Bay Area’s most promising startups. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 25,027.07, down 799.36 or 3.1 percent. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fared even worse, falling 283.09 or 3.8 percent, to close at 7,158.43. Most of the Bay Area's biggest tech stocks took a huge hit: Google parent Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOG) closed in New York at $1,050.82, down 55.61 or 5 percent; Facebook Inc. (NASDAQ: FB) ended the day at $137.93, down 3.16 or 2.2 percent; Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL) finished trading at $176.69, down 8.13 or 4.4 percent; Salesforce.com Inc. (NYSE:CRM) closed at $139.24, down 4.91 or 3.4 percent and Netflix Inc. (NASDAQ: NFLX) closed at $275.33, down 14.97 or 5.2 percent. Chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMD) plummeted 10.9 percent to $21.12. Larger rival Intel Corp. (NASDAQ: INTC) dropped 4.8 percent to $47.75. Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT) closed down 7.6 percent to $35.43. Seattle-based Amazon.com (NASDAQ: AMZN) finished at $1,668.40, down $103.96, or 5.9 percent. Outside of the tech arena, Wells Fargo & Co. (NYSE: WFC) closed at $51.78, down 2.46 or 4.5 percent, and Visa Inc. (NYSE: V) finished at $138.64, down $6.36, or 4.4 percent. There’s always hope that the increasingly volatile stock market will rebound, but investors for now are worried about trade tensions with China and uncertainty surrounding Great Britain’s exit from the European Union amid growing signs of a global slowdown. It doesn’t help that the nation’s real estate market is weakening. Bay Area real estate experts recently advised moving to cash and preparing for the next recession. “The housing market is no longer a tailwind for the U.S. economy. We believe housing sales have peaked and home price appreciation is forecast to slow, though not fall negative,” Bank of America Merrill Lynch (NYSE: BAC) said Tuesday in discussing its 2019 outlook. That may be cold comfort for homeowners in some markets already taking losses as they unload luxury homes in a cooling market. “While the Fed is trying to navigate the ever-elusive soft landing, it could find once fiscal stimulus wears off that it has raised rates too much, pushing the economy into a downturn,” Merrill Lynch said. That doesn’t bode well for initial public offerings, which depend on a strong stock market and an investor appetite for risk. No venture capitalist or other investors in private companies want to see billions in paper profits go up in smoke because a company tried to go public at a fire-sale price. For Bay Area residents, the losses go well beyond their stock portfolios. The money minted in IPOs is a key driver in the region’s economy, driving gains in home prices and in the value of employees’ stock options received as part of their compensation. – Senior Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Dec 4, 2018, 2:57pm PST Updated
